passages.text: A language does not die when its last speaker dies; by then it has been dead for a generation. The decisive moment comes much earlier and is almost invisible from outside: the point at which parents stop using it with their children. Everything that follows — the shrinking circle of fluent speakers, the shift of the language into ceremony and joke, the elderly woman photographed by a newspaper as the last of her kind — is the working out of a decision taken decades before, usually for reasons that had nothing to do with the language itself. Parents who switch are rarely rejecting anything. They are reading a labour market. This is why documentation and revival are not the same project and are often confused. A grammar and a sound archive preserve what a language was; neither creates a household in which a child hears it all day. Revival programmes that have succeeded have worked on the second problem, and they have all been expensive, slow and dependent on a community that had already decided it wanted the outcome.

Almost everything that determines the price of housing in a city was settled before the people now paying it were born. Zoning maps drawn in the 1920s and amended in the 1960s fix how tall a building may be, how many families may live on a plot and how much of that plot must be left empty. These rules were written by the residents of the time, for reasons that were often reasonable then, and they are enforced now against a population that was not consulted because it did not yet exist. The economics are not disputed: where supply is capped and demand is not, the price rises until enough people give up. What is disputed is who bears the cost, and here the accounting is unusual, because the people who bear it are mostly absent from the argument. They are the ones who did not move to the city, who commute two hours, or who are still living with their parents. No public meeting is attended by the household that was priced out four years ago.

Ask where a national dish comes from and the answer is usually a century old, not a millennium. The tomato reached most of the cuisines now unimaginable without it after 1500; the chilli did the same; and the dishes that a country teaches its children to regard as ancestral were in most cases codified between about 1880 and 1930, when cookbooks, railways and national feeling arrived together. This is not a debunking. A tradition that is a hundred and forty years old is still a tradition, and the cooks who wrote those books were usually recording something they had eaten rather than inventing it. What was new was the claim of nationality: the idea that a way of preparing a vegetable belonged to a country rather than to a valley. Historians of food therefore find themselves in an awkward position, because saying that a dish is younger than it is believed to be sounds like an accusation, and is generally received as one.

Until the railways, every town kept its own noon. Clocks were set by the sun where they stood, so that a town forty miles west of another was a few minutes behind it, and nobody was inconvenienced, because nobody could travel fast enough for the difference to matter. The railway made it matter. A timetable that meant one thing in one town and something else in the next was not a timetable, and after a number of collisions the companies imposed a single time along their own lines, which the towns they served eventually adopted. The interesting part is the resistance. Local time was felt to be a property of the place, like its weather, and to be told that noon was now an hour decided elsewhere was understood, correctly, as a transfer of authority. Courts in more than one country had to rule on which noon a contract referred to. What settled the question was not an argument but a habit: within a generation, the abolished local noon had been forgotten.

The written examination was invented to keep powerful families out of office. Imperial China used it for the better part of thirteen centuries, and when nineteenth-century British reformers borrowed the idea for their civil service, they borrowed it for the same reason: an anonymous paper, marked by a stranger, could not be a nephew. Both systems worked, in the narrow sense that they did what they were designed to do. Both also produced the complaint that has followed the examination ever since, which is that it selects not for the ability it names but for the ability to be examined — a related quality, distributed unevenly, and easier to buy than its defenders admit. The complaint is just, and it is not an argument for abolition, because the question is never whether the examination is a perfect instrument. It is whether the thing that would replace it, which is somebody's judgement of a candidate's promise, would be fairer. The historical record on that point is not encouraging.

questions.stem: The northern branch of the museum receives school groups almost every day, whereas ----.

options.o5: the decision had been taken by the previous council

questions.trap_note: Gerçekleşmemiş bir geçmişe gelecek zamanlı bir sonuç bağlar; koşulun geçmişte kaldığını görmez.

options.o5: existed only between towns that were very far apart

questions.why: Parça gerekçesiyle birlikte söyler: kimse rahatsız olmuyordu, çünkü kimse farkı önemli kılacak kadar hızlı yolculuk edemiyordu.
questions.trap_note: Nedeni ölçüm hassasiyetine bağlar; parçada fark ölçülemeyecek kadar küçük değil, önemsenmeyecek kadar etkisizdir.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the towns objected to a single railway time because ----.

options.o1: they understood it as authority passing to somewhere else
options.o2: the new timetables were difficult for travellers to follow
options.o3: the railway companies had not consulted the courts first
options.o4: collisions had gone on happening in spite of the change
options.o5: the clocks in most towns could not be adjusted at all

questions.why: Parça direnişi açıklarken 'doğru olarak, bir yetki devri diye anlaşıldı' der; itiraz pratik değil, siyasidir.
questions.trap_note: İtirazı bir kullanım güçlüğüne indirger; parça tam tersine, itirazın yerinde bir yetki okuması olduğunu söyler.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the dispute over local time ended ----.

options.o1: not because anybody was persuaded but because people grew used to it
options.o2: when the courts at last ruled on which noon a contract meant
options.o3: as soon as the railway companies had agreed among themselves
options.o4: after the last of the collisions had been investigated
options.o5: once clocks accurate enough to settle it had been invented

questions.why: Son cümle yanıtı verir: soruyu çözen bir sav değil, bir alışkanlıktır; bir kuşak içinde eski öğle vakti unutulmuştur.
questions.trap_note: Mahkemeler parçada sorunun bir belirtisi olarak anılır; kararların tartışmayı bitirdiği söylenmez.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.o1: Standard time was imposed as a practical necessity of the railways, resisted as a loss of local authority, and then forgotten.
options.o2: Railway collisions were caused by the fact that every town kept a noon of its own.
options.o3: Courts in several countries were unable to define what noon actually meant.
options.o4: Clocks were set by the sun until timepieces accurate enough to replace it appeared.
options.o5: The railway altered daily life more than any other invention of its century.

questions.why: Parça üç aşamayı sırayla anlatır: zorunluluk, direniş ve unutuluş; seçenek bu üçünü birlikte taşır.
questions.trap_note: Parçadaki bir ayrıntıyı ana fikir yerine koyar; çarpışmalar yalnızca tek saate geçişin gerekçesi olarak anılır.

questions.stem: According to the passage, nineteenth-century British reformers introduced the written examination in order to ----.

options.o1: keep appointments from being made inside families
options.o2: reproduce an institution that had worked in imperial China
options.o3: raise the standard of education throughout the country
options.o4: reduce the cost of recruiting officials to the service
options.o5: make certain that candidates were able to write clearly

questions.why: Parça amacı doğrudan yazar: yabancı birinin okuduğu imzasız bir kâğıt kimsenin yeğeni olamaz.
questions.trap_note: Aracı amaç yerine koyar; Çin örneği alınmıştır ama parça 'aynı nedenle' diyerek amacı ayrıca belirtir.

questions.stem: It is clear from the passage that the standing complaint about examinations is that ----.

options.o1: what they measure is the capacity to sit them
options.o2: they are marked by people who do not know the candidates
options.o3: they were designed for a society that no longer exists
options.o4: the preparation they require takes far too long
options.o5: they favour written ability over spoken ability

questions.why: Parça şikâyeti tanımlar: sınav adını taşıdığı yeteneği değil, sınava girilebilme yeteneğini seçer.
questions.trap_note: Parçada bu, şikâyet değil sistemin amacıdır: tanımayan birinin okuması kayırmayı engellemek içindir.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the writer regards the abolition of examinations as ----.

options.o1: a change that would have to be judged against whatever replaced them
options.o2: a reform for which the evidence of history offers clear support
options.o3: a matter that each country ought to settle for itself
options.o4: an outcome that powerful families would certainly resist
options.o5: a step that would lower the standard of the public service

questions.why: Parça soruyu yeniden kurar: sınavın kusursuz olup olmadığı değil, yerine geçecek olanın daha adil olup olmayacağı sorulmalıdır.
questions.trap_note: Tarihin verdiği desteği ters okur; parça kayıtların bu noktada 'iç açıcı olmadığını' söyler.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.o1: The examination is a flawed instrument that has survived because what would replace it is worse.
options.o2: Examinations ought to be reformed so that they no longer favour those who can pay.
options.o3: Britain took its civil service examinations directly from imperial China.
options.o4: Written examinations have been criticised in every society that has used them.
options.o5: Powerful families have always found ways of placing their relatives in office.

questions.why: Parça şikâyeti haklı bulur, kaldırmayı reddeder ve gerekçeyi alternatifin adaletine bağlar.
questions.trap_note: Parçanın vermediği bir reform önerisine atlar; metin sınavın düzeltilmesini değil, karşılaştırılmasını ister.

dialogue: You have been selling secondhand books in this street for thirty years. The internet was supposed to have finished shops like yours.
It finished the other kind. We used to make our money on the rare things, and anyone can now find a rare thing online in four seconds.
On what nobody knows they want. A customer comes in for one book and leaves with three, and no website has yet worked out how to do that.

options.o1: Then what is it that you make your money on now?
options.o2: So you have moved your rare stock online as well?
options.o3: How many shops of this kind are left in the city?
options.o4: Do you still buy books from private collections?
options.o5: Has the rent in this street risen much over that time?

questions.why: Yanıt 'On what ...' diye başlar ve bir şeyin neyden kazanıldığını söyler; boşluk da bunu soran cümledir.
questions.trap_note: Yanıt nadir kitaplardan söz etmez; dükkân sahibi bir önceki replikte o gelir kaynağının bittiğini söylemiştir.

dialogue: The city has added a charge of two euros a night to every hotel bill. Visitors say they are being punished for coming.
Two euros will not stop anybody coming. If it did, we would have learned something worth knowing.
To pay for the things that visitors use and residents pay for: the buses they take, the streets they walk along, the rubbish they leave behind.

options.o1: Then what is the charge actually for?
options.o2: So the aim is to bring the number of visitors down?
options.o3: How much does the charge raise in the course of a year?
options.o4: Do other cities in the country do the same thing?
options.o5: Will the charge be raised again next season?

questions.why: Yanıt 'To pay for ...' diye başlar ve bir amaç bildirir; boşluğa amacı soran cümle gelmelidir.
questions.trap_note: Yetkilinin bir önceki replikte reddettiği amacı yeniden önerir: iki euro kimseyi caydırmayacaktır.

dialogue: Your company now projects the text above the stage even when the play is performed in the audience's own language. Is that not something of an insult?
We thought so for years. Then we counted how much of the text an audience actually catches in a large house, and stopped arguing.
Rather less than the actors would like to believe. And the loss is not spread evenly: it falls on the quiet lines, which are usually the ones that matter.

options.o1: And how much does an audience catch?
options.o2: And did the actors agree with what you found?
options.o3: Was the experiment carried out in more than one theatre?
options.o4: Do the surtitles not distract the audience from the stage?
options.o5: Would a smaller house have made any difference?

questions.why: Yanıt bir miktar bildirir ve o miktarı oyuncuların beklentisiyle karşılaştırır; boşluk niceliği soran cümledir.
questions.trap_note: Yanıtta oyuncuların adı geçtiği için ilgili görünür; ama verilen şey bir onay değil, bir orandır.

dialogue: You spend your days looking at payments. What gives a fraudulent one away?
Almost never the amount. People expect us to watch for the large transfer, and the large transfer is the one thing a careful fraudster will not make.
The shape of the behaviour around it. An account that has paid the same four people for six years and suddenly pays a fifth, at three in the morning, from a city it has never been in.

options.o1: What is it that you watch for instead, then?
options.o2: So you set the threshold lower than people expect?
options.o3: How long does an investigation of this kind usually take?
options.o4: Are most of these payments recovered afterwards?
options.o5: Do the customers report the losses themselves?

questions.why: Uzman neye bakmadığını söylemiştir; yanıt ise neye baktığını anlatır, dolayısıyla boşluk bu karşıtlığı tamamlayan sorudur.
questions.trap_note: Konuyu yine tutara bağlar; oysa yanıt tutarı bütünüyle bırakıp davranış örüntüsüne geçer.

dialogue: You took over a club that had not produced a national finalist in twenty years, and you have produced four in five.
I changed almost nothing about the training. I changed who was in the room.
By going to schools that nobody else visits. The talent was never missing from this city; the scouting was.

options.o1: And how did you go about changing that?
options.o2: So the old training methods were at fault after all?
options.o3: How many athletes are training at the club now?
options.o4: Were the four finalists all competing in the same event?
options.o5: Is the club funded by the municipality?

questions.why: Yanıt 'By ...' ile bir yöntem bildirir; boşluk da bir işin nasıl yapıldığını soran cümledir.
questions.trap_note: Antrenörün açıkça dışladığı açıklamaya döner: antrenmanda neredeyse hiçbir şeyi değiştirmediğini söylemiştir.

questions.stem: Little did the organisers realise that the hall they had booked would hold barely half of those who came.

options.o1: The organisers had no idea that the hall they had reserved would take only about half of the people who turned up.
options.o2: The organisers were aware that the hall they had reserved would hold only half of those who came.
options.o3: Barely half of the people the organisers had expected came to the hall that was booked.
options.o4: The hall the organisers booked turned out to hold twice as many people as actually came.
options.o5: The organisers booked a small hall because they were expecting very few people.

questions.why: Little did + özne devrik yapısı bir bilgisizlik bildirir: düzenleyiciler salonun yetmeyeceğini hiç öngörmemiştir.
questions.trap_note: Devrik yapıyı olumlu okur; 'little' sözcüğü burada nicelik değil, olumsuzluk taşır.

questions.stem: The scheme was abandoned less because it was expensive than because nobody could explain what it was for.

options.o1: What brought the scheme to an end was not so much its cost as the fact that its purpose could not be explained.
options.o2: The scheme was abandoned mainly on account of its cost and only secondarily because its purpose was unclear.
options.o3: The scheme was expensive, but its purpose was perfectly clear to everyone involved in it.
options.o4: Nobody was able to explain why the scheme had turned out to be so expensive.
options.o5: The scheme would have been continued if it had been possible to reduce its cost.

questions.why: less because A than because B kalıbı ağırlığı B'ye verir: asıl neden amacın açıklanamamasıdır.
questions.trap_note: İki nedenin ağırlığını değiştirir; kalıbın hangi tarafı öne çıkardığı gözden kaçınca cümle tersine döner.

questions.stem: Far from settling the question, the new evidence has made both explanations harder to rule out.

options.o1: Instead of resolving the question, the new evidence has made it more difficult to eliminate either explanation.
options.o2: The new evidence has settled the question by ruling out one of the two explanations.
options.o3: The new evidence has confirmed both of the explanations that had been put forward.
options.o4: The question had already been settled long before the new evidence appeared.
options.o5: Neither explanation can be ruled out until further evidence has been found.

questions.why: Far from + ulaç kalıbı beklenenin tam tersini bildirir: kanıt çözmemiş, ayıklamayı zorlaştırmıştır.
questions.trap_note: Kalıbı olumlu okur ve kanıta soruyu çözdürür; 'far from' tam da bu okumayı engellemek için vardır.

questions.stem: Whatever the minister may say in public, the department has not changed its position.

options.o1: The department's position has remained the same, no matter what the minister says publicly.
options.o2: The minister's public statements have obliged the department to change its position.
options.o3: The department has changed its position without informing the minister of the fact.
options.o4: The minister says in public exactly what the department has already decided.
options.o5: The department will not change its position until the minister has spoken.

questions.why: Whatever ile kurulan ödün cümlesi bakanın söyledikleriyle bakanlığın tutumu arasındaki bağı koparır.
questions.trap_note: Ödünü bir nedene çevirir; cümle ise açıklamaların hiçbir etkisi olmadığını söyler.

questions.stem: A public library is judged by the number of books it lends, which is the one thing about it that is easy to count. ---- The room itself does work that no lending figure records: it is warm, it is free, it asks nobody why they have come, and in many towns it is the only address of that description. A service measured only by its loans will be cut in exactly the places where it is doing most.

options.o1: That figure, however, describes a small part of what the building is for.
options.o2: Loans have in fact been falling steadily for twenty years in most countries.
options.o3: Libraries of this kind were originally paid for by private benefactors.
options.o4: Staff are trained to help readers find what they are looking for.
options.o5: Most branches now lend films and recorded music as well.

questions.why: Boşluktan sonra ödünç sayısının kaydetmediği işler sıralanır; boşluk da o sayının eksikliğini bildiren cümledir.
questions.trap_note: Sayının yönünü tartışır, kapsamını değil; paragrafın savı ödüncün azalması değil, ölçüt olarak yetersizliğidir.

questions.stem: An institution that apologises for something done a century ago is regularly accused of making an empty gesture, and the accusation misses the point of such statements. ---- What an apology alters is the record: once it has been made, the thing apologised for can no longer be treated as a matter of opinion, and the institution's own archive becomes evidence against any later attempt to say otherwise. Whether that is worth anything depends on what is then done with it, which is a separate question.

options.o1: Nobody supposes that an apology repairs a harm done to people who are dead.
options.o2: Most such apologies are issued only after years of public pressure.
options.o3: Historians are rarely consulted before the wording is agreed on.
options.o4: Some institutions have apologised more than once for the same thing.
options.o5: The wording of these statements is usually prepared by lawyers.

questions.why: Boşluk, 'boş jest' suçlamasını kabul edip aşmalıdır: onarım beklenmediği söylenince paragraf özrün asıl işine geçebilir.
questions.trap_note: Özrün nasıl koparıldığını anlatır; paragrafın sorusu ise özrün ne işe yaradığıdır, nasıl elde edildiği değil.

questions.stem: A town that removes the signs, barriers and markings from a junction expects the junction to become more dangerous, and finds that it does not. ---- Drivers who cannot tell whose right of way it is slow down and look at one another, which is the behaviour the signs had been trying, without success, to produce. The effect does not survive being copied everywhere: what makes the bare junction work is that it is unusual.

options.o1: The reason is that uncertainty makes people careful.
options.o2: Most junctions of this kind carry very little traffic anyway.
options.o3: Experiments of this sort were first carried out in the Netherlands.
options.o4: Signs are expensive both to install and to maintain.
options.o5: Pedestrians are less confident at these junctions than drivers are.

questions.why: Boşluktan sonraki cümle beklenmedik sonucu açıklar; boşluk da o açıklamanın başlığını, yani belirsizlik ile dikkat arasındaki bağı vermelidir.
questions.trap_note: Sonucu açıklamak yerine örneği küçümser; paragraf ise kavşağın işlemesini sürücü davranışına bağlar.

questions.stem: A photograph of an event is treated as the least arguable kind of evidence, which is why editors choose them with such care. ---- The lens points somewhere, and everything outside the frame has been left out by somebody for reasons the reader is never told. A crowd of two hundred can be made to look like a crowd of two thousand by standing in the right place, and no part of the resulting picture is false. The argument, in other words, has been made before the reader sees anything at all.

options.o1: A photograph does not lie, but neither does it show everything.
options.o2: Photographs are now edited by software before they are published.
options.o3: Newspapers employ far fewer photographers than they once did.
options.o4: Readers remember pictures for longer than they remember text.
options.o5: The caption beneath a picture is written by somebody else.

questions.why: Paragraf fotoğrafın yalan söylemediğini ama çerçevesinin bir seçim olduğunu anlatır; boşluk bu iki yargıyı birden kurmalıdır.
questions.trap_note: Sorunu müdahaleye bağlar; oysa paragrafın örneğinde resmin hiçbir yeri sahte değildir, seçim çerçevededir.

sentences: The safety bicycle of the 1890s was cheap enough for a clerk to buy and simple enough for anybody to ride.
Within a few years it had done more for the freedom of movement of women than any argument made on their behalf.
Bicycle racing became a professional sport during the same decade.
Dress reformers had campaigned for years against skirts that made walking difficult, and had been ignored.
The bicycle settled the question by making the old clothing simply impractical.
questions.why: III. cümle bisikletin spor olarak gelişimine geçer; paragrafın anlattığı giyim tartışması ile bir ilgisi yoktur.
questions.trap_note: I. cümle giyimden söz etmediği için konu dışı sanılır; oysa bisikletin ucuzluğu ve kolaylığı, sonraki savın dayanağıdır.

sentences: The two-day weekend was not won in a single campaign; it was assembled out of two separate arguments.
The first was religious: factories employing both Jewish and Christian workers found it simpler to close on Saturday as well as Sunday.
The second was industrial: managers discovered that output over six days was not much greater than output over five.
By the 1930s the two arguments had arrived at the same place from opposite directions.
Public holidays vary considerably from one European country to another.
questions.why: V. cümle resmî tatillerin ülkelere göre farkına geçer; paragraf ise hafta sonunun iki ayrı gerekçeden nasıl kurulduğunu anlatır.
questions.trap_note: I. cümle bir genelleme gibi durur ama paragrafın yapısını kurar: 'iki ayrı sav' ifadesi sonraki iki cümlenin çerçevesidir.

sentences: A map is read as a description of the world, which is exactly what makes it such an effective argument.
The first printed maps of Europe appeared in the second half of the fifteenth century.
A border drawn as a firm line looks like a fact, even where the territory it crosses is disputed and the line is one party's claim.
Publishers who sell in several countries therefore print several versions of the same map, each of them legally required somewhere.
The reader of any one of them is being shown a position and told that it is a place.
questions.why: II. cümle basılı haritaların tarihine geçer; paragrafın 'harita bir betimleme değil bir sav taşır' zincirini ilerletmez.
questions.trap_note: IV. cümle yayıncılıkla ilgili bir ayrıntı gibi durur ama savın kanıtıdır: aynı haritanın birden çok yasal sürümü vardır.

sentences: The first cities to light their streets at night did so in order to reduce crime, and the effect on crime was modest.
The effect on everything else was not: shops stayed open later, theatres moved their performances back and a whole category of evening life came into being.
Gas was replaced by electricity in most European capitals around the turn of the century.
None of this had been intended by the authorities who paid for the lamps.
A measure adopted for one purpose had quietly rearranged the hours of the day.
questions.why: III. cümle aydınlatma tekniğinin değişimine geçer; paragrafın konusu ise beklenmeyen toplumsal sonuçtur.
questions.trap_note: I. cümledeki 'etkisi sınırlıydı' yargısı konu dışı sanılır; oysa paragrafın karşıtlığı tam da o sınırlı etki üzerine kuruludur.

sentences: Publishers resisted the cheap paperback for years on the ground that it would destroy the market for hardbacks.
The paper used in the earliest paperbacks was of poor quality and few copies of them have survived.
When one house finally tried it, the result was not a transfer of readers from one format to the other.
It was the appearance of a readership that had not been buying books at all.
The market the publishers had been protecting turned out to be smaller than the one they were refusing to enter.
questions.why: II. cümle kâğıt kalitesine ve nüshaların korunmasına geçer; paragraf ise cep kitabının pazarı nasıl büyüttüğünü anlatır.
questions.trap_note: IV. cümle tek başına okununca kopuk görünür; oysa III. cümlenin olumsuzladığı şeyin yerine geçen açıklamadır.
